timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Stewie, what is OWASP? I keep seeing it everywhere.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: OWASP stands for Open Worldwide Application Security Project. Their Top 10 is basically the 'most wanted' list of web vulnerabilities. It's updated every few years based on real-world breach data.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Like a criminal lineup for websites?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Exactly! And number one is Broken Access Control - when users can do things they shouldn't be able to do. Like viewing other users' data or escalating privileges.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Like when I accidentally see someone else's order on a website?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Precisely. That's an IDOR vulnerability - Insecure Direct Object Reference. It's embarrassingly common even in major applications. You just change the ID in the URL.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Injection attacks - SQL, NoSQL, OS command injection - are still in the top 5. Despite being known for over 20 years, they're still devastatingly effective.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: People still fall for SQL injection?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: More than you'd think. That's why parameterized queries exist. Never concatenate user input into queries. The MOVEit breach in 2023 was an SQL injection - billions in damages.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: XSS - Cross-Site Scripting - is another classic. Attackers inject malicious scripts into web pages. Stored XSS can affect every user who views a page.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Always. Name three OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities and explain how to prevent each one. If you can do that, you're ahead of most candidates.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Remember: the fundamentals stay the same. Input validation, output encoding, access control, and encryption. Trust nothing, verify everything.
